Two-way motion. One-way net flow. — Particles can cross either way

In this symmetric-crossing model, can particles go right to left while the left is more crowded?
column2:
Two-way motion. One-way net flow. — Particles can cross either way

Give every particle the same 20% crossing chance. With 48 starting on the left, expected traffic to the right is 9.6 per tick. With 12 on the right, expected traffic left is 2.4.

The decimals are averages across many repetitions. A single trial has whole particles.

Yes

Both directions remain possible. More particles starting on the left means more chances to cross right.

Random motion is two-way, even with a gradient.

column1:
Two-way motion. One-way net flow. — The difference is the net flow

For 48 left, 12 right and crossing chance 0.2, what is expected net traffic to the right per tick?
column2:
Two-way motion. One-way net flow. — The difference is the net flow

Subtract expected reverse traffic from forward traffic: 9.6 minus 2.4 gives a net 7.2 to the right. In equal volumes, the crowded side has the higher concentration.

7.2

Net to the right is 0.2 × 48 minus 0.2 × 12, which is 7.2.

Net flow is a difference, not the only direction of motion.

column1:
Two-way motion. One-way net flow. — An open barrier lets the imbalance shrink

Why does the expected net flow get smaller as the sides become similar?
column2:
Two-way motion. One-way net flow. — An open barrier lets the imbalance shrink

With a positive crossing chance, advance the model ticks. As the expected counts approach each other, the difference between the crossing rates shrinks. At zero crossing chance the barrier is closed and the imbalance stays fixed. Each tick updates both compartments, conserving all 60 particles.

The per-particle chance is unchanged, but the numbers of particles available on each side become more similar. Opposing traffic therefore becomes more similar.
  • Both directions still operate
  • Per-particle rule stays symmetric
  • Total particles are conserved

With positive crossing chance, the imbalance fades as opposing traffic balances.

column1:
Two-way motion. One-way net flow. — Balance does not mean motion stops

With equal concentrations and an open barrier, does zero expected net flow mean zero crossings?
column2:
Two-way motion. One-way net flow. — Balance does not mean motion stops

Start with 30 on each side. Expected crossings are 6 in each direction per tick, so net flow is zero. This is dynamic balance in the model.

Closing the barrier sets crossing chance to zero. That stops exchange through the barrier; it does not mean molecules stop moving within each side.

No

Equal expected traffic cancels in the net calculation, while crossings in both directions continue. Actual trials can fluctuate.

Zero net change can hide continuing two-way activity.
